walkthroughs.body_html: Cell 2 runs from Flamborough Head (north) to The Wash. Holderness lies within this cell, with cliffs of weak boulder clay (till) deposited during the last glaciation. Sediment moves south to feed Spurn Head spit and offshore Humber sinks.

Cliffs of unconsolidated boulder clay retreat at 1.8 m/yr on average, locally up to 10 m/yr. Around 29 villages have been lost since Roman times. Mappleton groynes (1991) trapped sediment north but increased downdrift erosion at Cowden, illustrating cell connectivity.

Spurn Head is a 5.5 km recurved spit at the Humber mouth, formed from southward longshore drift. The neck was breached in 2013 during a tidal surge, illustrating sediment supply vulnerability when updrift cliffs are protected.

mcqs.q: Why do some rivers form deltas and others form estuaries?
options: Deltas form where rivers deposit sediment faster than the sea can remove it (calm seas, heavy load); estuaries form where tidal energy removes sediment (strong tides).
Deltas form on big rivers and estuaries on small ones.
Plates move because of ocean tides pulling on the crust.
Deltas form in cold climates and estuaries in warm climates.

mcqs.q: What drives the movement of tectonic plates?
options: Plates move because of ocean tides pulling on the crust.
The Earth's rotation makes the plates move.
Convection currents in the mantle combined with slab pull at subduction zones and ridge push at constructive boundaries.
The three cells are tropical, temperate and arctic, named after climate zones.

mcqs.q: What are the three cells of global atmospheric circulation?
options: Plates move because of ocean tides pulling on the crust.
There is one big Hadley cell from the equator to each pole.
The Hadley cell (equator to 30 degrees), Ferrel cell (30 to 60 degrees) and Polar cell (60 degrees to poles) together redistribute heat from equator to poles.
